Amazon, Alphabet, and Microsoft together account for $120.8 billion in reported data center spending, more than twelve times Oracle's current run rate, concentrating physical AI infrastructure among three companies.

The spending gap reflects a shift in how AI scale is being pursued. The three leaders are building owned and operated facilities, while Oracle's $8.5 billion represents a different model, one that supplies infrastructure to others rather than consolidating it internally. CoreWeave at $7.7 billion occupies a middle position, offering specialized capacity. This divergence matters because it determines who controls the physical constraint: companies that own buildings and power systems set the pace of AI scaling, while service providers respond to demand they do not directly create.

The data covers reported capital expenditures as of mid-2026 and does not include off-balance-sheet financing, power purchase agreements, or land acquisition costs that do not immediately appear as spending. It also does not capture utilization rates, which determine whether announced capacity translates to usable compute. A company can spend heavily on buildings without filling them efficiently, or build incrementally while outsourcing peak demand. The true binding constraint on AI scaling emerges from comparing these numbers to grid capacity and construction timelines, neither of which this data provides.
